strengths: High-impact dataset and benchmark contribution: MMEarth-Bench provides 5 diverse, globally distributed environmental monitoring tasks (aboveground biomass, soil N, soil organic carbon, soil pH, and species occurrence) paired with 12 aligned modalities, filling a critical gap in existing geospatial benchmarks that typically provide few modalities and lack continent-wide geographic out-of-distribution splits.

Rigorous and extensive empirical evaluation: The authors benchmark 7 representative pretrained vision/EO foundation models (spanning RGB-only, multispectral, and multimodal architectures) across multiple data budgets (5%, 50%, 100%) and across both in-distribution and geographic out-of-distribution splits, providing valuable insights into geographic generalization and multimodal overfitting.

Novel and pragmatic formulation of Test-Time Training: Formulating multimodal data as self-supervised reconstruction targets during test-time adaptation (TTT-MMR) allows unimodal or multispectral pretrained models (e.g., RGB or Sentinel-2 only) to leverage multimodal context at test time without architectural redesign.

Effective domain-informed batching: The proposed geographic batching strategy (TTT-MMR-GEO) via spatial partitioning provides a principled compromise between domain specialization and gradient regularization in TTA, yielding consistent improvements over random batching across multiple tasks.

High clarity and reproducibility: The paper and extensive supplementary material detail the exact data curation protocols, filtering criteria, per-seed raw figures/tables, and inference efficiency measurements (<1 s per sample).
weaknesses: Limited comparison to single-modality TTT and modern TTA baselines: The main comparison is against the joint training (JT) baseline. Evaluating against single-modality masked autoencoder TTT (e.g., Gandelsman et al., 2022, reconstructing only the input modalities) would help isolate the specific performance gain attributable to multimodal auxiliary targets versus unimodal self-supervision.

Test-time data availability assumptions: The premise relies on having all 12 modalities accessible at inference time. While accessible globally via Google Earth Engine, real-time or bandwidth-constrained deployment pipelines may face challenges in acquiring all auxiliary data layers simultaneously.

Hyperparameter selection at test time: The optimal number of test-time update iterations is tuned using batches from the validation split. A brief discussion or ablation on sensitivity to iteration count and learning rate under strict online/streaming test-time settings without validation tuning would strengthen the practical takeaways.

strengths: Comprehensive and high-utility benchmark: MMEarth-Bench addresses prominent gaps in existing remote sensing benchmarks by providing 12 aligned modalities across 5 ecologically critical downstream tasks, evaluating both limited-data regimes and explicit out-of-distribution geographic generalization (held-out continent of Africa).

Novel and pragmatic formulation of Test-Time Training: The proposed TTT-MMR elegantly addresses the test-time modality mismatch problem by treating available test modalities as auxiliary self-supervised reconstruction targets rather than forcing them through the encoder. This allows unimodal/multimodal backbones to benefit from rich multimodal sensor data at inference in a model-agnostic manner.

Insightful analysis of geographic generalization: The empirical evaluation across 7 foundation models reveals key takeaways for the community—notably that multimodal finetuning can exacerbate geographic overfitting on certain domain-shifted tasks, and that existing global pretraining still suffers large geographic generalization drops.
Geographic batching insight: TTT-MMR-GEO provides a well-motivated spatial partitioning strategy that balances domain-specific adaptation with batch-level regularization.

Extensive documentation and reproducibility: The supplementary material is thorough, providing detailed data generation workflows, missing-data statistics, compute runtime analysis, linear probing baselines, and raw experimental tables.
weaknesses: Limited comparison to broader test-time adaptation baselines: The experimental validation compares TTT-MMR mainly against the Joint Training (JT) baseline and standard finetuning. While the authors discuss why methods like TENT (entropy minimization, batch norm updates) do not directly transfer to regression or non-BN ViTs, comparing against other architecture-agnostic TTA or domain adaptation strategies (e.g., self-supervised contrastive or feature-alignment approaches) would provide a stronger context.

Lack of modality ablation during test-time training: TTT-MMR reconstructs all 12 modalities simultaneously. It is unclear how sensitive adaptation performance is to the specific subset or type of modalities available at test time (e.g., pixel-level continuous vs. categorical vs. tile-level climate variables). An ablation showing performance when only a few modalities are available at test time would offer valuable practical insights.

Inference overhead and operational assumptions: Adapting the encoder at test time requires backpropagation per test batch (taking ~0.37s to 0.91s per sample as reported in Table S.8). While acceptable for offline analysis, this adds significant compute and latency compared to a standard forward pass (~0.002s - 0.009s), and assumes continuous access to 12 synchronized modalities at inference.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated benchmark: MMEarth-Bench addresses critical deficiencies in existing Earth Observation (EO) benchmarks by providing 5 distinct global environmental tasks (biomass, soil nitrogen, organic carbon, pH, and species distribution) paired with 12 aligned modalities and a rigorous out-of-distribution geographic test split (Africa).

Thorough empirical evaluation: The paper benchmarks seven recent foundation models spanning RGB-only, multispectral (Sentinel-2), and multimodal architectures across multiple data regimes (5%, 50%, 100%) under both finetuning and linear probing.

Valuable empirical findings: The study demonstrates that while multispectral and multimodal pretraining improves low-data performance in-distribution, geographic generalization to held-out continents remains very poor across all models, and incorporating multimodal inputs during finetuning can paradoxically exacerbate geographic overfitting.

Effective, model-agnostic test-time adaptation: TTT-MMR leverages available test-time modalities as self-supervised reconstruction targets rather than inputs, allowing models with rigid input spaces to benefit from auxiliary multimodal signals without architectural alterations. The geographic batching variant (TTT-MMR-GEO) is well-reasoned and consistently balances regularization with regional adaptation.

High level of rigor and reproducibility: The paper includes extensive ablation studies, per-seed statistics, detailed dataset generation pipelines, timing benchmarks, and an interactive data explorer tool in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Practicality of auxiliary modality availability at test time: The framework relies on the assumption that up to 12 modalities are available at test time to serve as reconstruction targets. While achievable via Google Earth Engine, in constrained or real-time deployment settings, acquiring and preprocessing 12 synchronous modalities creates a significant operational bottleneck.

Substantial test-time latency overhead: As reported in Table S.8, TTT-MMR requires full backpropagation through the encoder for several gradient steps per batch, increasing inference latency by roughly two orders of magnitude (e.g., from 0.007s to 0.910s per sample for DINOv3 Sat). The trade-off between this computational cost and downstream accuracy gains should be more thoroughly discussed.

Limited comparison against existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods: While the paper justifies why classification-specific methods like TENT are inapplicable to continuous biophysical regression, it lacks comparisons with other general regression-compatible TTA or self-supervised adaptation baselines (such as unimodal masked reconstruction TTT or test-time feature alignment), primarily comparing against Joint Training (JT).

Modest absolute gains on challenging tasks: While Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirm statistical significance, the absolute improvement on certain out-of-distribution splits is relatively small (e.g., R² improvements of 0.01–0.03 for soil properties), and negative R² values on Soil OC persist even after adaptation.

Limitations of IUCN species range data: Using IUCN mammal range polygons as ground truth for tile-level presence/absence is prone to commission errors (predicting presence where local habitat is unsuitable), which can introduce label noise into the species occurrence benchmark.

strengths: Comprehensive and timely benchmark (MMEarth-Bench) targeting critical limitations in Earth Observation (EO): evaluating multimodal foundation models under true geographic domain shifts (held-out continent of Africa) and low-shot regimes across five real-world environmental tasks.

Extensive evaluation across 8 modern pretrained geospatial and vision foundation models (ranging from unimodal RGB to multispectral and multimodal architectures), providing realistic and candid insights (e.g., the strong performance of randomly initialized multimodal baselines with sufficient data, and the severe geographic generalization gap across models).

Creative use of multimodality at test time via TTT-MMR: instead of ignoring modalities incompatible with the pretrained encoder input, the method leverages them as auxiliary reconstruction targets for test-time adaptation.

Domain-grounded batching technique (TTT-MMR-Geo) using spatial partitioning, which effectively balances specialization and regularization, demonstrating clear benefits on long-tailed target distributions.

Thorough experimental validation and documentation in the appendix, including multi-seed evaluations, linear probing vs. fine-tuning analyses, modality ablation, and detailed dataset curation statistics.
weaknesses: TTT-MMR is not fully post-hoc / test-time-only; it requires joint training (JT) of an auxiliary task modality decoder alongside the task head during downstream supervised fine-tuning before test-time adaptation can be conducted.

The absolute performance gains of TTT-MMR over the joint training baseline are relatively modest on several tasks/models (e.g., typically 0.005–0.01 improvements in R^2 or mAP, as shown in Table A.17).

Comparison against existing test-time adaptation (TTA) baselines is limited: while the paper discusses methods like TENT and masked-autoencoder TTT in related work, empirical comparisons are primarily restricted to the JT baseline rather than existing adaptation or self-training baselines adapted for regression/multimodal settings.

Practical deployment considerations: TTT-MMR relies on collecting and aligning 12 auxiliary modalities at test time, which could incur computational and data retrieval overhead in real-time inference pipelines.

strengths: High-impact benchmark contribution (MMEarth-Bench): The paper introduces a comprehensive, standardized multimodal benchmark spanning five ecologically vital tasks (biomass, soil N, soil OC, soil pH, and species distribution) paired with 12 aligned satellite, environmental, and climate modalities across global geographic scales.

Rigorous experimental design and split setup: Unlike many existing Earth observation benchmarks that evaluate on random spatial crops or localized regions, MMEarth-Bench explicitly formalizes a continental held-out split (Africa) alongside data-fraction tiers (5%, 50%, 100%), rigorously testing both low-shot transfer and out-of-distribution geographic generalization.

Extensive and revealing empirical evaluation: Benchmarking 8 recent foundation models (Scale-MAE, DINOv3, SatlasNet, MPMAE, TerraMind, Copernicus-FM, Galileo) alongside from-scratch baselines uncovers key domain insights—notably that most pretrained models fail significantly on geographic shifts and that training a multimodal model from scratch can match or beat complex global pretraining when labeled data is sufficient.

Sound and model-agnostic test-time adaptation methodology (TTT-MMR): Formulating test-time auxiliary tasks via multimodal reconstruction enables models to benefit from all test-available modalities without requiring multimodal encoder architectures. The per-modality gradient normalization is technically sound and prevents gradient domination.

Insightful geographic batching (TTT-MMR-Geo): Adapting batches grouped by spatial proximity via recursive spatial partitioning provides a meaningful balance between regularization and specialization, demonstrating pronounced benefits on the long-tail/rare sample distributions.
weaknesses: Requirement of auxiliary modalities at test time: TTT-MMR operates under the assumption that all 12 modalities are readily available at inference. While this fits the benchmark setting, fetching and preprocessing numerous sensor, climate, and elevation products in practical, low-latency deployment scenarios could introduce non-trivial overhead.

Prerequisite of Joint Training (JT): The method requires training a modality decoder alongside the primary task decoder during the supervised fine-tuning phase. Consequently, it cannot be applied directly as a plug-and-play TTA technique to arbitrary, already deployed off-the-shelf checkpoints without retraining with joint reconstruction losses.

Modest absolute performance gains on top models: While improvements are shown to be statistically significant, the absolute improvements on top-performing models (e.g., Table A.17) are quite small on several tasks (e.g., delta R² below 0.01 for soil OC and pH), indicating that the test-time signal primarily refines rather than drastically transforms the representations.

Single-region evaluation for geographic shift: The out-of-distribution evaluation is restricted exclusively to Africa as the held-out target region. Evaluating across multiple held-out regions or a leave-one-continent-out protocol would provide a more complete assessment of out-of-distribution robustness.

strengths: High-impact benchmark contribution (MMEarth-Bench): The benchmark directly tackles three pervasive bottlenecks in geospatial machine learning—limited labeled data, geographic domain shifts (evaluating explicitly on an entire held-out continent, Africa), and sensor ambiguities—by providing 12 aligned modalities across five global environmental tasks.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking: The authors evaluate 8 prominent foundation models (spanning RGB-only, multispectral Sentinel-2, and multimodal architectures) alongside randomly initialized baselines across three training data regimes (5%, 50%, 100%), yielding valuable empirical insights (e.g., that an untrained multimodal model can be highly competitive with pretrained models given sufficient data).

Novel adaptation formulation (TTT-MMR): Repurposing multimodal reconstruction tasks as test-time training signals is elegant and architecture-agnostic. The per-modality gradient normalization is technically sound and avoids gradient domination across disparate continuous and categorical loss scales.

Effective spatial inductive bias (TTT-MMR-Geo): Introducing geographic batching via recursive spatial partitioning provides a well-motivated compromise between domain specialization and gradient regularization, demonstrating clear benefits on long-tailed/rare target distributions.

Rigorous documentation and reproducible experimental design: The manuscript and extensive appendix (including ablation studies on modality importance, iteration counts, and per-modality reconstruction performance across multiple seeds) demonstrate exceptional thoroughness.
weaknesses: Test-time compute overhead: TTT-MMR requires iterative gradient computation and backpropagation during inference (0.37s–0.91s per sample vs. <0.01s for standard forward passes, a ~100x increase). For global remote sensing inference spanning millions of tiles, this computational overhead poses practical deployment challenges.

Assumption of full auxiliary modality availability at test time: The framework relies on having access to auxiliary modalities at test time to serve as reconstruction targets. While the authors demonstrate leave-one-out robustness in the appendix, a more systematic study on adaptation degradation under sparse or partially missing test-time modalities would further strengthen the practical claims.

Limited comparison to modern test-time adaptation baselines: Comparisons are largely centered against the Joint Training (JT) baseline. Benchmarking against adapted versions of competitive test-time adaptation approaches (e.g., pseudo-labeling/conjugate pseudo-labeling or feature-entropy minimization where applicable) would more clearly isolate the specific advantage of multimodal reconstruction over generic TTA.
